Article Title: UP Creators Summit & Awards to celebrate the state's rising digital voices and creator economy in grand 2-day event
Article Text:
Times of India’s UP Creators Summit & Awards

Honouring the creators shaping a new Uttar Pradesh

Conversations driving the future of the creator economy

Preparing creators for the future

As India's creator economy continues to redefine entertainment, entrepreneurship and storytelling, Uttar Pradesh is emerging as one of the country's fastest-growing hubs for digital innovation. With increasing internet penetration, a thriving startup ecosystem and the rapid rise of creators from Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, the state is playing a pivotal role in shaping India's digital future.Celebrating this transformation, the inaugural edition Times of India’s UP Creators Summit & Awards will bring together some of the state's most influential content creators, industry leaders, brands and digital innovators for a 2-day mega showcase of recognition, insightful conversations and future-focused learning.To be held on August 19 and 20 in Varanasi, the spiritual and cultural heart of Uttar Pradesh, the event will bring together the state’s rich heritage and its new-age digital voices, showcasing how creators are shaping the narrative of a new Uttar Pradesh. The first day, August 19, will feature insightful masterclasses, panel discussions and fireside chats, while August 20 will culminate in the grand UP Creators Awards, celebrating the state’s most impactful digital creators.At the heart of the event are the Creators Awards, which will honour creators who are making a meaningful impact across diverse genres, including education, technology, finance, food, travel, lifestyle, comedy, fashion, gaming, social impact and more. These creators are not only building communities online but are also amplifying local stories, inspiring millions and showcasing Uttar Pradesh's talent on the national and global stage. The awards celebrate creators who are redefining digital influence while contributing to the state's growing reputation as a powerhouse of innovation and creativity.Beyond the awards, the summit will serve as a platform for thought-provoking discussions on the opportunities and challenges shaping the creator ecosystem.Panel discussions will explore how the creator economy is expanding beyond metropolitan cities into Tier 2 and Tier 3 India, the growing influence of creators in rebranding Uttar Pradesh, and the role of digital storytellers in building the narrative of a new Uttar Pradesh. The event will also feature engaging fireside chats on themes such as "Storytellers of a New Bharat" and "Beyond Followers", examining how creators are moving beyond metrics to create meaningful impact, influence culture and build sustainable careers.As artificial intelligence reshapes the content landscape, the summit will host a dedicated AI Masterclass on future-proofing content creation. The session will provide practical insights into how creators can leverage AI-powered tools to enhance creativity, improve productivity and stay ahead in an increasingly competitive digital ecosystem.Bringing together creators, policymakers, industry experts and ecosystem enablers, the UP Creators Summit & Awards aims to celebrate the diverse voices driving India's digital revolution while highlighting Uttar Pradesh's emergence as one of the country's most exciting creator hubs. More than just an awards platform, the summit will spotlight the ideas, conversations and collaborations that are shaping the future of content creation in India.
Article Summary: Times of india’s up creators summit & awards will be held on august 19 and 20 in varanasi, the spiritual and cultural heart of uttar pradesh. The event will honour creators who are making a meaningful impact across diverse genres, including education, technology, finance, food, travel, lifestyle, comedy, fashion, gaming, social impact and more.

Article Title: GOBARdhan scheme: How India plans to turn cattle dung, crop waste and garbage into fuel
Article Text:

The bigger picture

For years, India has spoken about the enormous amount of energy locked inside its agricultural residue, cattle dung and organic waste. The challenge has been turning that potential into a commercially viable industry.Now, the government is making one of its most serious attempts yet.The Union Cabinet on August 6 approved GOBARdhan, the National Circular Bioenergy Scheme, with a total outlay of Rs 23,731 crore for FY 2026-27 to FY 2035-36. The scheme has set a target of ten-fold increase in domestic production of Compressed Biogas (CBG) and brings together everything from assured demand and pricing to capital assistance, pipelines and credit under a single framework.The idea sounds simple: take waste that would otherwise be burnt, dumped or left to decompose, and process it in a biogas plant and turn it into fuel that can be used much like natural gas.But the government's ambition goes much further.It wants villages to become centres of energy production, farmers to become suppliers to the energy industry and organic waste to become an economic resource rather than a disposal problem.The question is whether the new scheme can solve the problems that have held back India's CBG industry for years.GOBARdhan is not an entirely new idea.The initiative was originally launched in 2018 under the Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen as a waste-management programme. Its focus was on converting cattle dung, kitchen waste, crop residue and other organic material into biogas and bio-slurry, helping villages manage waste while generating useful products.The 2026 version is much broader.The government has now positioned GOBARdhan as a national framework for the Compressed Biogas industry, bringing several existing measures under one umbrella and placing the scheme under the ministry of petroleum and natural gas.These include the Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation (SATAT) initiative, the Market Development Assistance scheme for organic manure, the Biomass Aggregation Machinery scheme, pipeline infrastructure support and central financial assistance for CBG plants.In simple terms, the government is moving from “how do we manage organic waste?” to “how do we build an industry around it?”The process begins with organic material such as cattle dung, agricultural residue, press mud from sugar mills and municipal organic waste.This material is fed into an anaerobic digester, where microorganisms break it down in the absence of oxygen and produce biogas. The raw biogas contains methane along with carbon dioxide and other impurities.The gas is then purified to remove these impurities and compressed.The resulting Compressed Biogas, or CBG, has properties comparable to natural gas and can be used within the existing gas ecosystem. This is one of its biggest advantages: India does not necessarily need to create an entirely separate fuel infrastructure for it.The process also produces organic material that can be processed into fertiliser.That means one plant can potentially create several economic outputs:Waste → CBG + organic manure + rural jobs + additional income opportunitiesThis is the circular economy the government is trying to build.The biggest reason is energy security.India currently imports nearly 50% of its natural gas requirement, according to the government's latest GOBARdhan backgrounder. That leaves the country exposed to international gas prices, shipping disruptions and geopolitical shocks.Domestic CBG offers a way to produce a portion of that gas from resources that India already has in abundance.The government estimates that lower dependence on imported fossil fuels under GOBARdhan could eventually save more than Rs 40,000 crore in foreign exchange. That is a government projection rather than a guaranteed saving, but it illustrates the scale of the ambition.There is also an environmental argument.Agricultural residue that is not economically used can become a waste-disposal problem, while organic waste dumped in landfills can generate methane and other emissions. Converting such material into fuel gives it an economic value while potentially reducing waste-related emissions.For farmers, the attraction is an additional market for residue and dung.For energy companies, it is another source of domestic gas.For the government, it is a way of connecting waste management, rural development and energy security.This is where the GOBARdhan story becomes more complicated.India's push for CBG production predates the new scheme by several years.The government launched SATAT in October 2018, with an ambitious target of establishing 5,000 CBG plants producing 15 million tonnes a year.But the industry struggled to scale at the pace initially envisaged.A 2022 review by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas found that against the target of 5,000 plants by 2023-24, only 40 had been set up at that point. The committee also highlighted problems with financing, multiple approvals, pricing and feedstock availability.One of the biggest problems was that a CBG plant needs much more than a piece of land and a digester.It needs a reliable supply of biomass, equipment to collect and transport that biomass, storage facilities, technology, financing and, crucially, a buyer for the gas.One big complication with agricultural residue is that it is seasonal.Crop waste may be available in large quantities for only a few months of the year, forcing plants to invest in storage and logistics if they want to operate throughout the year. The parliamentary committee specifically flagged this issue.Bansal estimates that India generates around 230 million tonnes of surplus agricultural residue annually, suggesting that the problem is not a shortage of biomass but the difficulty of turning dispersed and seasonal supplies into a reliable, year-round feedstock chain.GOBARdhan's focus on biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure and district-level planning is therefore critical to making plants operate at high utilisation.There was also a financing problem.Banks and investors were wary of projects whose revenues depended on uncertain feedstock supplies and evolving CBG prices. The committee noted concerns over the low internal rate of return of plants and called for more remunerative pricing.This is the gap GOBARdhan is now attempting to close.Kapil Bansal, partner, energy transition and decarbonization at EY-Parthenon India, told TOI that the biggest change is that GOBARdhan tackles the entire CBG value chain rather than individual bottlenecks.Earlier measures addressed issues such as biomass aggregation, organic manure, pipelines and financial assistance separately, but developers continued to face uncertainty around demand, pricing and financing.“The sector is moving from a project-led approach to a market-led approach, where demand, pricing and financing visibility are available before developers invest,” Bansal said.The combination of assured offtake, a ten-year pricing framework, capital assistance, pipeline connectivity and credit guarantees, he said, should improve project bankability and give investors greater confidence.The government has structured GOBARdhan around six major components, each designed to address a different weakness in the existing CBG ecosystem.1. Assured demand for CBGPerhaps the biggest change is that producers will have greater certainty that someone will buy their gas.City Gas Distribution companies will procure CBG in line with a notified obligation that rises from 3% in FY 2026-27 to 4% in FY 2027-28 and 5% from FY 2028-29 onwards for the CNG transport and PNG domestic segments.This creates a predictable demand signal.For investors, that matters because a plant is much easier to finance when there is greater clarity about who will buy its output.GOBARdhan introduces a government-backed CBG price of Rs 2,110 per MMBTU, with a minimum ten-year framework.The objective is to give producers greater revenue visibility and make projects more attractive to investors and lenders.This directly addresses one of the problems identified in the earlier CBG ecosystem: uncertainty over whether the economics of a plant would work after it was built.Eligible greenfield CBG projects will receive capital assistance of up to Rs 2 crore for every tonne per day (TPD) of installed capacity.Importantly, the support is not restricted to the core plant.It can also cover critical assets linked to feedstock aggregation, organic manure processing and value addition. Brownfield projects expanding existing capacity will also be eligible.That matters because the economics of CBG depend on the entire supply chain, not just the digester.A CBG plant cannot be commercially successful if its gas cannot reach the market.GOBARdhan therefore provides for cluster-based and standalone pipeline infrastructure connecting plants with trunk pipelines and City Gas Distribution networks.The aim is to reduce evacuation costs, improve reliability and expand the market available to producers.The scheme also attempts to solve the financing problem through a dedicated credit guarantee mechanism.By sharing part of the lending risk, the government hopes banks will be more willing to finance MSME-based CBG projects.This could bring smaller companies, cooperatives, women entrepreneurs and first-time developers into an industry that has so far been dominated by larger players and institutional initiatives.The final component focuses on the problem that often receives the least attention: where will the feedstock come from?The CBG Ecosystem Challenge Fund will support biomass mapping, aggregation infrastructure, district-level development plans, technology adoption, process improvements and organic manure value addition.The objective is to build the local ecosystem around each plant rather than treating the plant as an isolated piece of infrastructure.The government's larger pitch is that farmers should become participants in India's energy economy.Crop residue and cattle dung can become feedstock for CBG plants, creating potential additional income for farmers and local aggregators.The benefit does not stop with the gas.The material left after the biogas production process can be processed into organic fertilisers such as Fermented Organic Manure and Liquid Fermented Organic Manure.This creates a second revenue stream while returning nutrients to agriculture.The government has already been supporting this side of the industry through the Market Development Assistance scheme. Together, these measures are intended to create a cycle in which agricultural and livestock waste becomes an input for both energy and agriculture.That is why GOBARdhan is being presented as more than an energy scheme.It is also a rural infrastructure and waste-management programme.This is perhaps the most revealing part of the government's latest numbers.As of August 6, the GOBARdhan Unified Registration Portal had recorded 1,908 registered CBG/Bio-CNG plants. Of these, 217 had been commissioned, while another 339 were under construction, according to the government.The numbers show both the opportunity and the problem.There is considerable interest in building CBG capacity, but the number of plants actually operating remains far below the number registered.The government says the various initiatives introduced over recent years have helped commission more than 200 CBG plants and establish the initial production and offtake ecosystem. GOBARdhan is now intended to take that foundation to a national scale.In other words, the new scheme is not starting from zero.It is an attempt to make the existing pipeline of projects commercially viable and scalable.That remains the biggest question.Government support can reduce the initial cost of a plant and create a market for its gas. But it cannot eliminate the fundamental logistical challenge of collecting biomass.Bansal cautioned that commercial viability will still vary from project to project because feedstock costs, transportation distances, plant utilisation and financing costs will continue to determine returns.“A project with reliable access to high-quality feedstock can achieve significantly better plant efficiency and returns than a project relying on dispersed or lower-yield biomass resources,” he said.A plant located far from its feedstock source may face high transportation costs. Agricultural residue is seasonal. Competing uses for biomass can raise prices. Plants also need to maintain reliable operations and consistent gas quality.These problems were highlighted by the Parliamentary Standing Committee even before the latest scheme was announced. It pointed to the uneven availability of feedstock, the need for storage and the importance of synchronising CBG production with the national gas grid.This is why the six components of GOBARdhan matter together.A subsidy without a buyer does not solve the problem.A buyer without a pipeline does not solve the problem.A pipeline without reliable feedstock does not solve the problem.And a plant with all three still needs affordable financing and efficient operations.GOBARdhan is effectively trying to solve all of these problems at the same time.The government has set an ambitious ten-year vision.It expects GOBARdhan to deliver nearly ten-fold growth in domestic CBG production, attract large private investment, create rural employment and expand the organic fertiliser economy. It also projects lower fossil-fuel use and significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.These are targets and government projections, not guaranteed outcomes.The more important test will be whether the number of operating plants grows alongside registrations, whether plants remain viable after initial assistance and whether farmers and local businesses actually benefit from the new demand for biomass.If that happens, GOBARdhan could change the economics of waste in India.Instead of paying to collect, transport and dispose of organic waste, communities could potentially build local industries around it.India's CBG journey has already shown that having abundant biomass is not enough.The country had an ambitious 5,000-plant target under SATAT, but financing constraints, feedstock logistics, approvals, pricing uncertainty and weak project economics slowed the industry's development.GOBARdhan is the government's attempt to address those weaknesses through one national framework.At Rs 23,731 crore over ten years, the bet is substantial.But the real significance of the scheme is not the size of the allocation. It is the attempt to connect India's farms, villages, waste streams and gas networks into one economic system.If the model works, cattle dung and crop residue will no longer be treated merely as waste. They could become feedstock for a domestic fuel industry, while the by-products return to farms as organic fertiliser.That would turn the government's “waste-to-wealth” slogan into a functioning business model.The challenge is making sure the economics work beyond the subsidy period.For GOBARdhan, success will therefore not be measured simply by how much money is spent or how many plants are registered. It will be measured by how many plants actually operate, how much CBG they produce, whether farmers earn from supplying biomass and whether India's dependence on imported gas falls.India has plenty of waste. GOBARdhan now has to prove that it can turn that waste into a dependable source of energy, income and economic value.
Article Summary: The union cabinet on august 6 approved gobardhan, the national circular bioenergy scheme. The scheme has set a target of ten-fold increase in domestic production of compressed biogas (cbg) it brings together everything from assured demand and pricing to capital assistance, pipelines and credit under a single framework.

Article Title: Reliance to partner Rolls-Royce to develop fighter jet engines
Article Text:
The AMCA is being developed as a twin-engine, medium-weight stealth fighter for the Indian Air Force.

NEW DELHI: In a boost to India's fifth gen fighter programme, Mukesh Ambani 's Reliance Industries Ltd and Rolls-Royce Friday announced they plan to jointly develop a sovereign indigenous combat engine for India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA).As part of the partnership to design, develop, manufacture and deliver the same, Reliance and Rolls-Royce will explore formation of a dedicated aerospace gas turbine complex that will be a centre for power and propulsion technology in India.The aero gas turbine complex will build sovereign, end-to-end Indian capability across design, development, manufacturing, testing, production and through-life support, while unlocking wider collaborations across defence, civil aerospace, and new power and propulsion systems.Aeronautical Development Agency under DRDO is officially designing and managing the AMCA project. As per initial planning, ADA is progressing with imported US GE F414 engines for the initial five AMCA prototypes under the Rs 15,000-crore programme. TNN
Article Summary: The amca is being developed as a twin-engine, medium-weight stealth fighter for the indian air force. Reliance and rolls-royce will explore formation of a dedicated aerospace gas turbine complex that will be a centre for power and propulsion technology in india.

Article Title: Cockroaches, expired food: Maharashtra FDA suspends 14 licences linked to Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart
Article Text:
Inspections uncovered violations ranging from cockroach infestation and expired food to poor hygiene and storage practices.

NEW DELHI: The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has suspended the licences of 14 food business establishments linked to quick-commerce platforms Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart after a statewide inspection drive uncovered multiple food safety and hygiene violations.The August 13 drive covered 86 establishments across Maharashtra involved in the storage, sale and delivery of food through online platforms. The FDA issued 60 improvement notices and ordered one facility to temporarily halt operations, news agency PTI reported.Of the 14 suspended licences, five were linked to Blinkit, five to Zepto, two to Instamart, while one each belonged to Bhagwati Stores and Swinsta Ent Pvt Ltd.The inspections focused on storage conditions, temperature control, cleanliness, pest management, personal hygiene of food handlers, food safety records, display of licences and compliance with inventory practices such as First In, First Out (FIFO) and First Expired, First Out (FEFO).In Pune, the FDA suspended the licence of a Zepto outlet in Lohegaon after inspectors found food items stored beyond their declared "use by" dates.The regulator also flagged unhygienic storage conditions, inadequate pest control and lapses in personal hygiene, adding that the company's response during the hearing was unsatisfactory.Another Pune facility operated by Swinsta Ent Pvt Ltd was found to have a cockroach infestation, inadequate cold-chain maintenance for frozen products and deficiencies in hygiene and pest-control practices.In Mumbai, a Blinkit facility in Malad (West) was found to be operating with chiller temperatures above the prescribed limit. Inspectors also found that around 40 food handlers had not undergone mandatory medical examinations and that records were unavailable.The FDA said several workers were not using protective gear such as gloves, aprons and head coverings. Inspectors also found damaged storage racks, poor organisation and inadequate segregation of different categories of food products.At another Blinkit facility in Ghatkopar, officials flagged shortcomings in drainage, waste disposal, temperature control and housekeeping. The outlet was classified as non-compliant after scoring 46 per cent during the inspection.Inspections at Zepto facilities in Mulund and Goregaon revealed deficiencies related to food storage, temperature management, cleanliness and licence display.At an Instamart outlet in Andheri, inspectors found food packets stored directly on the floor. The FDA also reported inadequate storage space, overcrowding and deficiencies in hygiene and temperature control.The inspection drive also covered delivery operations.At a Blinkit store in Karad in Satara district, officials checked 125 delivery riders and found that they lacked identity cards and medical fitness records. The regulator also found that the outlet's FSSAI licence was not displayed on delivery bags and boxes.The FDA directed the company to suspend two-wheeler delivery operations at the outlet until the deficiencies were addressed.The regulator said the action was taken under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and urged all food businesses operating through online platforms to strictly comply with prescribed food safety, hygiene and storage standards.
Article Summary: Inspections uncovered violations ranging from cockroach infestation and expired food to poor hygiene and storage practices. Maharashtra food and drug administration (fda) has suspended the licences of 14 food business establishments linked to quick-commerce platforms blinkit, zepto and instamart.

Article Title: Govt scraps 12-minute ad cap for TV channel
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Television channels will no longer be restricted to 12 minutes of advertisements per hour, with the government deciding to scrap the two-decade-old cap in a move it says will put traditional broadcasters on a more level footing with digital platforms.The restriction, introduced in 2006 under the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, will cease to apply once the amended rules are notified in the Gazette, the information and broadcasting ministry said.The government has argued that the television landscape has changed substantially since the cap was imposed. India had only 62 TV channels in 2006, compared with more than 900 now. Cable television, then the dominant distribution platform, was largely analog and offered limited capacity and consumer choice.With digitisation, platforms including cable TV, direct-to-home, HITS and IPTV can now carry 300 to 500 channels or more, significantly expanding viewer choice and competition, the ministry said.The decision could give broadcasters greater flexibility to determine advertising inventory, an important consideration for an industry that remains heavily dependent on advertising revenue across both pay and free-to-air channels.The ministry also cited the growing competition television faces from digital media, where there is no comparable statutory cap on advertising duration.It said the existing restriction had created a “non-level playing field” for conventional television broadcasters and that removing it would promote “fair competition” and ease of doing business.The change, however, will become operational only from the date the amendment to the Cable Television Networks Rules is formally notified.
Article Summary: The restriction, introduced in 2006 under the cable television networks rules, 1994, will cease to apply once the amended rules are notified in the gazette. The government has argued that the television landscape has changed substantially since the cap was imposed. India had only 62 tv channels in 2006, compared with more than 900 now.

Article Title: 5 indigenous small modular reactors targeted by 2033, Jitendra Singh tells LS
Article Text:
Union MoS Jitendra Singh speaks in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon session of Parliament

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A key objective of the govt under the Nuclear Energy Mission is to develop and operationalise at least five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033, minister for department of atomic energy Jitendra Singh said in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday.Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is undertaking the design and development of indigenous SMR technologies, including the 220 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor (BSMR-200) and 55 MWe SMR-55 for power generation. BARC is also developing a high temperature gas cooled reactor (HTGCR) of up to 5 MW capacity, which can be coupled with a suitable thermochemical cycle for hydrogen production.Singh said India is steadily strengthening its indigenous nuclear energy ecosystem with a focus on advanced reactor technologies, SMRs, domestic manufacturing capabilities, private-sector participation and long-term utilisation of the country’s abundant thorium resources. The govt has adopted a two-pronged approach to accelerate nuclear capacity addition. This includes deployment of large indigenous reactors such as 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs) and advanced reactor designs at greenfield sites, alongside development and deployment of SMRs at brownfield locations, including retiring fossil-fuel-based power plants, captive plants for energy-intensive industries and off-grid applications in remote areas.The minister also highlighted continuing work of the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) in advancing the second stage of India’s nuclear power programme. IGCAR is pursuing multidisciplinary scientific research and advanced engineering development for sodium cooled fast breeder reactors and associated closed fuel-cycle facilities, technologies that remain a cornerstone of India’s long-term nuclear strategy.On thorium, Singh said India is pursuing its three-stage nuclear power programme, based on a closed fuel cycle, to optimise utilisation of its uranium resources and progressively harness its abundant thorium reserves. Thorium, being a fertile material, needs to be converted into fissile uranium-233 in a nuclear reactor before it can be used for energy generation.India has already undertaken sustained R&D towards thorium utilisation. Thorium Oxide (Thoria) pellets have been used in the initial cores of operating PHWRs, while Thoria-based fuels have also been irradiated in BARC research reactors. The irradiated Thoria pins have been reprocessed to obtain uranium-233, which has subsequently been fabricated as fuel for the KAMINI reactor at IGCAR, Kalpakkam. Singh said the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, 2025 has been enacted to enable wider participation of both public and private entities in the nuclear sector.
Article Summary: The govt under the nuclear energy mission is to develop and operationalise at least five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033. Bhabha atomic research centre (barc) is undertaking the design and development of indigenous smr technologies. The govt has adopted a two-pronged approach to accelerate nuclear capacity addition.

Article Title: 800 kmph in 5.3 seconds: China train sets third record in six months
Article Text:
The 1,110-kg test vehicle, developed at Donghu Laboratory, achieved the milestone in its latest trial

How China’s experimental maglev works

Why reaching 800 kmph is so difficult

Could maglev technology launch rockets?

China has pushed maglev technology into a speed range far beyond conventional high-speed rail, with an experimental train car reaching 800 kmph in only 5.3 seconds on a 1-km test track in Hubei.The 1,110-kg test vehicle, developed at Donghu Laboratory, achieved the milestone in its latest trial, marking its third world record in six months.The experiment, however, is not aimed at putting passengers on trains travelling at 800 kmph.Instead, the technology could eventually have applications in rocketry, military aircraft, drones and industrial transport, where extremely rapid acceleration could be more useful.Unlike conventional trains, maglev vehicles use magnetic forces to reduce or eliminate physical contact between the train and the track. Electromagnetic systems can both levitate the vehicle and propel it forward.China's fastest commercial maglev service, the Fuxing system, has a top speed of about 217 mph (349 kmph. The experimental Donghu Laboratory vehicle is therefore operating at more than twice that speed.The latest test was carried out on a 1-km-long track in Hubei. According to CGTN, the system worked like a giant slingshot: magnetic forces propel the vehicle forward while eliminating the friction associated with conventional rail travel.The test vehicle has already broken its own short-distance acceleration record multiple times. Its first public run in June 2025 reached about 404 mph (650 kmph) in 7.1 seconds.Engineers subsequently raised the speed to about 433 mph (697 kmph) before reaching nearly 496 mph (798 kmph) in November.At such speeds, even tiny deviations in the track can become a major engineering challenge.The experimental system reportedly requires track alignment to remain within 0.5 millimetres.Control systems must simultaneously manage the vehicle's position, levitation and electromagnetic propulsion while maintaining stability during rapid acceleration.The vehicle weighs around 1,110 kg, meaning enormous amounts of energy and force are required to accelerate it to such speeds within seconds.The trials have also helped researchers test technologies involving high-power energy delivery, levitation control, positioning, electromagnetic propulsion and emergency braking.The biggest significance of the experiment may lie beyond railways.Passenger trains travelling at such speeds would require expensive infrastructure and enormous energy inputs, while acceleration levels involved in the tests would not be suitable for conventional commuter travel.Researchers are therefore exploring whether similar electromagnetic acceleration technology could eventually be adapted for rockets, drones and military aircraft.A ground-based launch system capable of giving a rocket or aircraft a substantial initial boost could potentially reduce the amount of fuel it needs to carry for take-off. Similar technology could also find applications in industrial transport and specialised elevators.For now, the technology remains experimental. China's commercial maglev systems already demonstrate that magnetic levitation can deliver very high-speed passenger transport, but the leap from those systems to an 800-kmph experimental vehicle represents a very different engineering challenge.
Article Summary: The 1,110-kg test vehicle, developed at donghu laboratory, achieved the milestone in its latest trial. Electromagnetic systems can both levitate the vehicle and propel it forward. The technology could eventually have applications in rocketry, military aircraft, drones and industrial transport, where extremely rapid acceleration could be more useful.

Article Title: Who is Gautam Rangarajan? Indian-origin strategist appointed to key role by UK PM Andy Burnham
Article Text:
Indian-origin strategist Gautam Rangarajan.

Who is Gautam Rangarajan ?

What will Gautam Rangarajan do at No. 10?

Burnham's government overhaul

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Indian-origin strategist and former BBC executive Gautam Rangarajan as an Expert Adviser on Structure and Process in a newly created role at 10 Downing Street.Rangarajan, who brings decades of experience in strategy, organisational transformation and media, is set to take up the position this week.Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive with more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting.Before his new government role, he spent more than 30 years at the BBC, beginning his career as a radio music producer and eventually rising to become the broadcaster's Group Director for Strategy and Performance.His experience includes developing strategy in rapidly changing markets, leading large-scale transformation initiatives and handling complex policy and financial negotiations.The exact details of Rangarajan's responsibilities are yet to be outlined. However, the UK PM's office said his appointment draws on his experience in corporate strategy and transformation.His role comes as Burnham undertakes a broader restructuring of the machinery of government, including the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.Rangarajan is expected to play a role in the planned transformation at the heart of the British government.Away from strategy and public service, Rangarajan also has a creative side. He describes himself as a professional choral singer and music producer, alongside his work in corporate strategy and organisational transformation.The appointment comes as Burnham reshapes his government following his recent rise to the role of Labour Party leader and Prime Minister.His administration has announced structural changes, including the launch of No. 10 North in Manchester and the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.While the full scope of Rangarajan's new role remains unclear, his appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.
Article Summary: Indian-origin strategist gautam rangarajan appointed as expert adviser on structure and process at 10 downing street. Article Title: Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox: "I think the scariest person in the world is the person with…" - a lesson on humour, perspective and facing hard times with lightness
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox (AP photo)

Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox

"I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor"

Where this quote actually comes from

Why humour matters most during genuinely difficult stretches

How humour actually helps people manage stress

Why laughing at your own mistakes actually matters

Why humour can genuinely strengthen relationships

Michael J. Fox's own perspective on adversity

Why humour is not the same thing as avoiding a real problem

Why being naturally serious is not actually a flaw

Other memorable quotes by Michael J. Fox

"One's dignity may be assaulted, vandalized and cruelly mocked, but it can never be taken away unless it is surrendered."

"I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection."

"Family is not an important thing. It's everything."

"Acceptance doesn't mean resignation; it means understanding that something is what it is and that there's got to be a way through it."

Why people still find meaning in this quote

Humour can genuinely change how a difficult moment actually feels. A stressful situation seems lighter once someone finds a reason to laugh, and a serious problem often becomes easier to approach once it can be seen from another angle. It can create a little distance from fear, frustration and uncertainty, even when the circumstances themselves have not changed. Michael J. Fox , the actor and Parkinson's disease advocate, put a striking twist on that idea. "I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor," he said. Not being able to laugh, in his framing, is not simply a personality quirk. It genuinely limits how someone can respond to life, and coming from someone who has lived with a serious, lifelong illness for decades, the line carries a good deal more weight than a passing joke.This line comes from an interview Fox gave to journalist Amy Wallace, published on Reader's Digest's website. Fox is not really suggesting that a humourless person is dangerous in any literal sense. He is pointing at the seriousness that tends to surround someone who cannot laugh at themselves, cannot recognise irony, and cannot find any lightness in a genuinely difficult moment. Humour creates real distance from a problem.It lets someone acknowledge that something is hard without letting it completely take over.Life inevitably brings disappointment, uncertainty and real stress. Humour cannot solve every problem on its own, but it can genuinely change how someone responds to one. Being able to laugh during a hard period offers a small emotional break, and it can help people communicate when a direct, serious conversation feels too uncomfortable to actually have. None of this means every situation deserves to be treated as a joke. Humour and genuine seriousness can exist side by side.Stress tends to narrow someone's attention down entirely onto the immediate problem in front of them. A moment of real laughter can interrupt that cycle. Research into humour and stress has suggested that positive humour can genuinely influence mood and help people cope with stressful experiences, and laughter itself is linked to physiological changes, including a release of muscle tension. None of this should be overstated. Humour is never a substitute for professional help or a practical solution when someone faces a genuinely serious problem. As an everyday coping tool, though, it can offer a genuinely useful shift in perspective.One of the most valuable forms of humour is simply being able to laugh at your own missteps. Nobody gets everything right. People mispronounce words, misjudge situations and occasionally embarrass themselves, and someone who can acknowledge a mistake without being consumed by embarrassment tends to find it easier to actually learn from it. Self-directed humour also tends to make social interactions considerably more comfortable, since it signals that a person does not expect flawless perfection from either themselves or anyone else around them.Shared laughter helps people form real connections. Friends, colleagues and family members often use humour to build a sense of familiarity and trust, and a well-placed joke can break tension that a serious conversation might struggle to shift on its own. There is an important line here worth being clear about, between humour that actually brings people together and humour that humiliates someone else. Jokes built on cruelty or prejudice tend to damage relationships rather than genuinely strengthen them, and the most constructive kind of humour has never really needed anyone else to get hurt.Fox became one of the most recognisable actors of his generation through films and television, including Back to the Future and Family Ties. In 1991, at the age of 29, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. He later made the diagnosis public and became a prominent advocate for Parkinson's research through the Michael J. Fox Foundation. His public approach to living with the condition has consistently included honesty, genuine optimism and humour, which gives his comments about laughter an extra dimension. His point was never that difficult experiences are inherently funny. It is that holding onto a sense of humour can help someone preserve real perspective while actually facing a genuine challenge.There is a meaningful difference between using humour to cope with something difficult and using it to avoid actually dealing with it at all. Some problems genuinely require serious attention and real action, and nobody can simply laugh away financial difficulty, illness or grief. What humour can offer instead is a small amount of emotional breathing space while someone continues addressing the actual underlying issue, which is really the whole distinction worth holding onto here.Fox's quote is deliberately provocative, and it should not be read as suggesting that serious people are inherently unpleasant. Some people naturally have quieter personalities, or simply express humour in a different way. The broader lesson is really about flexibility rather than personality type. Someone who can be genuinely serious when it matters, while still finding moments of humour elsewhere, tends to have more ways of responding to life's challenges than someone who treats every single situation with exactly the same level of weight.Humour is easy to underrate, since it can look insignificant next to more obviously serious qualities like intelligence or discipline. Even so, the ability to laugh genuinely shapes how people communicate, handle their own mistakes and respond to real difficulty. Fox's quote offers a deliberately provocative reminder that life does not always need to be approached with complete seriousness. There will be moments when humour is genuinely inappropriate, and problems that cannot be laughed away at all. In between those moments, though, holding onto a sense of humour tends to keep people connected, flexible and hopeful, which is really the whole point behind the line.
Article Summary: "i think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor" michael j. Fox, actor and parkinson's disease advocate. Not being able to laugh is not simply a personality quirk. It genuinely limits how someone can respond to life. Actor michael j. Fox was diagnosed with parkinson's disease in 1991.

Article Title: OpenAI ‘loses’ another top executive as chief revenue officer Denise Dresser resigns: Read her Linkedin post
Article Text:
Read Denise Dresser’s full post on LinkedIn

Team,

I wanted to let you know that I made the difficult decision to leave OpenAI in the coming weeks to pursue other opportunities.

The opportunity to work hands-on with the most transformative technology in the world has been nothing short of incredible. I am so proud of what we have accomplished and, even more, of how this team has shown up for our customers and one another.

Thank you for your trust, your partnership, your hard work, and the energy you bring every day. You’ve kept an extraordinary pace, all while staying focused on delivering value for our customers. No one works harder than this team. I’m deeply grateful to every one of you.

I’ve been working with @gdb to ensure a smooth transition as we’ve discussed the future needs of the business. He will share more about those plans shortly. I will still be here for a bit continuing to partner with the team and our customers as we make this change.

If you need anything, please reach out on Slack anytime.

OpenAI sees high-stakes departure ahead of IPO

OpenAI chief revenue officer Denise Dresser is stepping down after less than a year with the ChatGPT-maker, adding to a wave of high-profile leadership departures as the firm prepares for an anticipated initial public offering (IPO). OpenAI said that Dresser is leaving to “pursue other opportunities.” To fill the vacancy, the company has appointed Dali Rajic, former President and Chief Operating Officer of cybersecurity firm Wiz, as its new Chief Revenue Officer, as per a report by CNBC.Dresser confirmed her resignation in a post on LinkedIn, expressing gratitude for her time leading the company's enterprise expansion.“Sharing the note I sent to the team today. I’m incredibly proud of all we’ve accomplished together and deeply grateful to the extraordinary people and customers who made this chapter so meaningful. I’m excited for what lies ahead and will be cheering this remarkable team on every step of the way,” she said in a post on LinkedIn.Dresser’s resignation arrives at a critical operational moment for OpenAI. The company confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, following a funding round that valued the startup at $852 billion. Hired in December after more than a decade as an executive at Salesforce, Dresser was tasked with accelerating OpenAI's commercial revenue and competing against chief rival Anthropic for lucrative corporate contracts.Dresser is the second top executive to exit OpenAI this week, following Brad Lightcap’s announcement that he was departing the company to launch a new venture. The recent string of high-level exits includes Fidji Simo, the former product and business chief who stepped down last month due to health recovery.Brad Lightcap, who served as COO, an eight-year OpenAI veteran, announced his resignation on Tuesday. Three senior executives, including former head of the Sora video division Bill Peebles, departed the company in April.
Article Summary: Denise dresser is the second top executive to exit openai this week. The company has appointed dali rajic, former president and chief operating officer of cybersecurity firm wiz, as its new chief revenue officer. Dresser was hired in december after more than a decade as an executive at salesforce.

Article Title: Instagram gets first logo update in 10 years, internet jokes it now reads 'Instagzam'
Article Text:
Instagram's new logo

Instagram head Adam Mosseri says it was time for a refresh

Internet quickly pokes fun at new Instagram logo

Meta-owned photo sharing platform Instagram has rolled out its first logo update in a decade. But the redesign is already drawing mixed reactions online. While Meta says the new wordmark is "cleaner and more modern," many users have joked that the updated lettering makes the app's name difficult to read. Some said it looks like "Instagzam," while others compared it to "Instagwam" and even questioned whether the new design meets accessibility standards. The app's familiar multicoloured camera icon remains unchanged, with only the wordmark at the top of the app getting a new look.Announcing the redesign, Instagram head Adam Mosseri said the company wanted to modernise the logo after keeping it unchanged for 10 years.“The wordmark at the top of the app hasn't changed in 10 years, so it was time for a refresh,” Mosseri wrote in an Instagram post. He added, “Cleaner and more modern, with references to the original and the simplicity and craft that's always made it Instagram.”Mosseri also shared the announcement on Threads, writing, "Thought I'd share this on Threads [too] and see what the hot takes might be."The redesigned wordmark quickly became a talking point on Instagram and X (formerly Twitter), with many users saying some of the letters are difficult to recognise.One user commented, "Is it just me or It reads : instagzam ❓."Another wrote, "Instagwam – how a toddler would pronounce it. Perfect."Others joked that the logo looked like "Instaguam," while another user said, "It's barely readable. Does it even pass accessibility checks? Booo. I might be the outspoken minority, but do not like."While the logo attracted plenty of attention, some users said Instagram should focus on other issues affecting the platform. "Adam, while Instagram gets a new look, thousands of legitimate creators and businesses are losing their accounts without clear explanations or real support," said one user responding to Mosseri’s post.
Article Summary: Instagram has rolled out its first logo update in a decade. Many users have joked that the updated lettering makes the app's name difficult to read. The app's familiar multicoloured camera icon remains unchanged, with only the wordmark at the top of the app getting a new look.

Article Title: Phoebe Gates’ shopping app Phia responds to 'cookie stuffing' allegations, says have started issuing ...
Article Text:
Phoebe Gates' Phia responds to cookie stuffing allegations

What Phia spokesperson said

What is cookie stuffing that Phoebe Gates’ Phia is accused of

Phia, the AI-powered shopping startup founded by Bill Gates daughter Phoebe Gates and her Stanford roommate Sophia Kianni said that it is reviewing every transaction carefully and will reverse sales that were incorrectly attributed to it, says a report by People. The development comes days after a Bloomberg report said that the two founders were aware of ‘cookie stuffing’ – a practice where affiliate tracking cookies are placed on a user's browser without their knowledge, allowing a company to claim commission on purchases even when it did not influence the sale. The report cites internal Slack messages, people familiar with the matter and historical source code saying that both Gates and Kianni were aware of automatic cookie-setting features months earlier.The People report quotes a Phia spokesperson who told the publication:“Any features causing misattributions were immediately removed over a month ago on July 7. We are reviewing every transaction, we are fully committed to and have already begun issuing all transaction reversals to brand partners as a result of any misattribution, and we are hiring a head of compliance to make sure something like this never happens again.”“We are now continuing to connect our users with items and offers from thousands of brand partners,” the spokesperson continued, further adding “We will learn from this and want to ensure our users have the best possible shopping experience, with features like our new digital closet and more to come.”The statement did not address Bloomberg’s latest accusationsPhia operates as a browser extension designed to help shoppers automatically find discount codes and compare prices at online checkout counters. In exchange, partner retailers pay the platform an affiliate commission when its software helps convert a sale.However, internal chats accessed by the publication reveal that Phia implemented automated features that injected its tracking cookies into a shopper’s checkout session without requiring any user interaction, such as clicking a deal link or applying a coupon code, the Bloomberg report said. By dropping tracking identifiers automatically, Phia claimed credit and commissions for transactions it did not drive, a practice widely known as cookie stuffing and that is strictly prohibited by commercial network contracts and partner agreements.
Article Summary: Phoebe gates' phia responds to cookie stuffing allegations. Spokesperson: we are reviewing every transaction, we are fully committed to and have already begun issuing all transaction reversals to brand partners. Bloomberg report said that the two founders were aware of ‘cookie stuffing’

Article Title: China takes aim at Elon Musk’s ‘Jesus-level’ brain-chip dream with first BCI surgery policy
Article Text:
Repesentative image

A first-of-its-kind insurance policy

How the technology works

The 'Jesus-level technology'

Clinical trials in China and safety concerns

Government push

Elon Musk has spent years pursuing what he has called "Jesus-level" technology through Neuralink, aiming to treat chronic health conditions by implanting computer chips directly into the human brain. But that vision may end up taking shape fastest not in the US, but in China, where state authorities have launched a coordinated push to accelerate the country's own brain-computer interface (BCI) industry, according to a South China Morning Post report. China has introduced its first commercial policy covering invasive brain-computer interface (BCI) surgery. State-owned PICC Property and Casualty announced the scheme in partnership with a hospital affiliated with Zhejiang University School of Medicine in Hangzhou, a tech hub home to leading AI and robotics start-ups.Over the past few days, a string of BCI-related initiatives have been announced across China, involving state insurers, investment banks and local governments alike. The most significant came on Wednesday, when PICC Property and Casualty, a major state-owned insurer, announced it had signed the country's first commercial insurance policy covering the invasive surgery typically required to implant a BCI device in a patient's brain.The announcement moved markets almost immediately, with BCI-linked stocks in Hong Kong climbing as investors bet that insurance coverage would help speed up the technology's path to commercial use. Shares of BCI-related firms rose 1.59% on Wednesday, with neuro-interventional device maker Shanghai Heartcare Medical Technology up 1.28% and software developer BrainAurora Medical Technology gaining 1.65%.BCI technology, which conventionally involves open-skull surgery to implant electrodes in a targeted region of the brain, allows patients to control digital devices using thought alone. The field has been most prominently championed globally by Musk's Neuralink, and versions of the technology have already been tested on human patients in both the US and China, in some cases showing promise in helping patients paralysed from the neck down regain the ability to move.The public hospital involved in PICC's new insurance scheme is regarded by local officials and doctors as a leading centre for BCI clinical trials in the region, and has reportedly conducted at least 12 human trials involving BCI implants, according to Chinese media reports. In one recent case, a 61-year-old paraplegic patient with a spinal cord injury regained the ability to bend and lift his leg within three days of surgery, and was walking unassisted by the fifteenth day.Brain-computer interfaces allow signals generated by the brain to be converted into digital commands that can control computers, devices or prosthetics. Musk has repeatedly promoted the technology's potential to transform lives. Speaking via video link at an event in Israel this week, Musk argued that his company, Neuralink, does not receive enough recognition for its achievements."Restoring control of people who are tetraplegics and restoring sight, I think, are pretty big deals," Musk said. "They're sort of what I might call Jesus-level technologies," he added. Neuralink has said its implants could eventually allow users to type, move a computer cursor and operate devices using only their thoughts. Supporters of the technology envision an even more ambitious future, where people could communicate digitally through thoughts or interact with machines without physical input.BCI technology, championed by Elon Musk’s Neuralink, requires open-skull surgery to implant electrodes that allow patients to control digital devices with their thoughts. In Hangzhou, doctors have conducted at least 12 human trials. In one case, a 61-year-old paraplegic regained the ability to walk unassisted within 15 days of surgery.Clinicians cautioned that safety must remain the top priority. “We don’t yet have long-term safety data from BCI clinical trials. There’s no data spanning several years,” said Duan Wanru, chief physician at Xuanwu Hospital in Beijing, during the Global Health Summit in Hong Kong.Alongside the insurance policy, the Zhejiang provincial government announced plans to boost financing for BCI firms and encourage them to go public. The coordinated effort underscores China’s ambition to lead in brain-computer interface technology, potentially outpacing Musk’s vision of “Jesus-level” implants to treat chronic conditions.
Article Summary: China has introduced its first commercial policy covering invasive brain-computer interface (bci) surgery. State-owned picc property and casualty announced the scheme in partnership with a hospital affiliated with zhejiang university school of medicine in hangzhou. In hangzhou, doctors have conducted at least 12 human trials.

Article Title: America’s biggest investor Michael Burry, who warned Wall Street of 2008 housing crisis, is not happy with Oracle and Micron, here's why
Article Text:
Michael Burry’s concerns about Oracle

The AI hype problem of Micron

Michael Burry is not happy with reports of Nvidia investing $250 billion in OpenAI

America’s biggest investor Michael Burry who famous for warning about the 2008 housing crisis has taken aim at two major technology players Oracle and Micron Technology. According to a report by The Street, known for his contrarian bets, Burry argues that both companies are overexposed to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom and weighed down by financial commitments that could backfire if demand slows.As per the report, Burry disclosed a short position against Oracle, highlighting its massive spending on AI infrastructure. The company has signed long-term leases and GPU capacity contracts worth hundreds of billions, far exceeding its current revenue base. Despite the strong operating cash flow, Oracle reported negative free cash flow due to surging capital expenditures. Burry warns that if AI demand falters, Oracle could be left with costly obligations and declining returns.Micron Technology is also in Burry’s crosshairs. He expanded his short bet against the chipmaker, arguing its recent rally is driven more by investor enthusiasm for AI than by solid fundamentals. Micron has historically struggled with cyclical downturns, and Burry believes its profitability remains vulnerable despite the current boom.Burry’s bearish stance extends beyond individual companies. He has also shorted the iShares Semiconductor ETF and Nebius Group, signaling broader doubts about the sustainability of AI-linked stocks.His thesis centers on off-balance-sheet liabilities: companies committing billions to long-term infrastructure at inflated prices, which could become burdensome if growth slows.Recently, Michael Burry voiced his sharp criticism of reports that Nvidia is preparing a a $250 billion backstop for OpenAI’s massive Ohio data-center project. According to a report by the Wall Street journal, the guarantees would help OpenAI lease a 10-gigawatt site being developed by SoftBank’s SB Energy, with total costs potentially exceeding $500 billion. Burry’s complaint echoes what analysts have long warned about in AI megadeals: circular funding arrangements that expose investors to enormous risk if sentiment shifts or growth slows. Nvidia, already valued at $5 trillion, has invested $30 billion in OpenAI and is now considering financing chip purchases worth another $350 billion. Critics say such structures could leave the industry vulnerable, especially since OpenAI remains unprofitable and lacks an investment-grade credit rating.Michael Burry’s criticism underscores growing unease about the sustainability of $100 billion-plus AI financing structures. His warning suggests that while AI demand is surging, the industry’s reliance on complex guarantees and debt-backed megaprojects could become its biggest vulnerability.
Article Summary: America’s biggest investor michael burry has taken aim at two major technology players oracle and micron technology. Burry argues that both companies are overexposed to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom and weighed down by financial commitments that could backfire if demand slows.

Article Title: Oracle layoffs: As Oracle leadership prepares to send ‘6am layoff email’ on September 1, company asks managers to give a list of…
Article Text:
Oracle cut 21,000 jobs last year. Another round is coming this month

Oracle layoffs in March arrived as 6AM emails for 10,000+ employees and ended the same working day

Oracle has burned through almost all of its $2.1 billion restructuring budget

Why Oracle's $55.7 billion AI data centre spending keeps the pressure on headcount

Oracle is lining up another round of job cuts this month, and the deadline is set by its own calendar. Managers have been asked to draw up lists of employees whose roles are being eliminated, with the company looking to bring payroll down before September 1—the day its fiscal second quarter opens. Business Insider, which first reported the plan citing people familiar with it and an internal document, said reductions on some teams could reach double-digit percentages.The cuts would land on top of a year in which the company already removed about 21,000 full-time roles, roughly 13% of its workforce. Headcount fell from around 162,000 in May 2025 to about 141,000 at the end of May 2026, with roughly 49,000 of those remaining in the United States. What makes this round sting is Oracle's own explanation. Its annual filing attributes part of the decline to the company's adoption and deployment of AI—the same technology it is borrowing tens of billions of dollars to sell.Employees cut on March 31 found out first thing in the morning. The notification, sent from "Oracle Leadership," told recipients their role had been eliminated as part of a broader organisational change and that it was their last working day.Staff in both the US and India were affected. LinkedIn posts from those let go pointed to Oracle Health, Sales, Cloud, Customer Success and NetSuite. Roughly 10,000 positions went in that single wave.The email itself was brisk. It thanked employees for their contributions, told them severance paperwork would arrive via DocuSign, and asked them to submit a personal email address immediately—because access to their computer, email and files was about to be switched off.Severance is not cheap. Oracle booked $1.8 billion in restructuring costs in FY2026, up from $374 million a year earlier, a 391% jump. Its 10-K, filed on June 22, capped the total expected cost of the plan at $2.1 billion, which leaves only about $300 million of headroom. Cuts at the scale Business Insider describes would either have to fit inside that remainder or push Oracle into its second new restructuring plan in three years. TD Cowen analysts estimated in January that shedding 20,000 to 30,000 workers could unlock $8 billion to $10 billion.The money is going somewhere specific. Capital expenditure hit $55.7 billion in FY2026, up from $21.2 billion the year before, as Oracle raced to build data centres for customers including OpenAI. It raised $43 billion in debt and $5 billion in equity over the year, expects around $40 billion more in FY2027, and ran free cash flow of negative $23.7 billion. Interest expense alone climbed to $4.6 billion from $3.6 billion.The underlying business is not the problem. FY2026 revenue rose 17% to $67.4 billion, cloud infrastructure revenue grew 77%, and remaining performance obligations closed the year at $638 billion after ending Q3 at $553 billion. Oracle has also told investors that AI code generation is letting it reorganise product development into smaller teams, saying the technology helps it build "more software in less time with fewer people. "That sentence, written for shareholders in March, reads differently in August. Investors have not been won over either—the stock is down more than 20% this year, and shareholders sued in January over what Oracle said about how much it would need to borrow to service its $300 billion OpenAI commitment.For the employees on this month's lists, the reasoning is beside the point. The jobs are being removed to meet a date on a fiscal calendar, and the payoff Oracle is betting on will arrive after they have gone.
Article Summary: Oracle has burned through almost all of its $2.1 billion restructuring budget. The company cut 21,000 full-time roles last year, roughly 13% of its workforce. It attributes part of the decline to the company's adoption and deployment of ai.

Article Title: Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings on why he stopped calling CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters about the business: They can mimic me and...
Article Text:
Reed Hastings on leaving the Netflix board: 'like being a godparent versus a parent'

The Warner Bros. Discovery call Netflix made without its founder in the room

Netflix's co-founder Reed Hastings spent 29 years at Netflix and now sends its two CEOs almost nothing. Not because anything soured — the opposite. He says Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters have absorbed his thinking so completely that phoning them is redundant. He's tested that theory in the biggest way possible. When Netflix walked away from the Warner Bros. Discovery deal this year, its founder wasn't in the room for the call.Speaking on Semafor's The CEO Signal podcast, hosted by Penny Pritzker and Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson, the Netflix co-founder said he's been "very disciplined" about not calling the co-CEOs on business matters since leaving the board in June. He tried, briefly. For the first couple of months he lobbed in the occasional thought, then noticed something: they could already run the simulation without him. They ask what Reed would think, set that answer aside, and do what they believe is right. Which, Hastings said, is what they should do. "They can mimic me and conjure me easily. I'm very predictable in that way."The social side hasn't gone anywhere—he still talks to them and they hang out.What changed was the front line. Hastings stepped down as Netflix CEO in January 2023 and left the board this June, and he's blunt that the second exit was the smaller one. Being on a board of a company doing well, he said, is a fairly relaxed gig. The genuinely disorienting part was the workload dropping from around 70 hours a week to roughly one.The clearest proof of the handover came this year, when Netflix walked away from the Warner Bros. Discovery deal. Hastings says he wasn't involved in that decision at all. Sarandos and Peters worked the trade-offs themselves. He describes it as a price question rather than a strategy one—Netflix was comfortable with what it had offered, Larry Ellison raised the bid, Netflix had the chance to match and chose not to.Hastings frames the whole shift as moving from parent to godparent. The company, he added, has to stop reliving how he did things and start making its own mistakes.

He says ted sarandos and greg peters have absorbed his thinking so completely that phoning them is redundant. When netflix walked away from the warner bros. Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.
